1:
Keil and Delitzsch place the chapter first: this is the last revelation Daniel received about the future of his people, unfolding the hostile attitude of the world-power toward the kingdom of God from the Persian dominion to the end of the days, together with the protection the covenant people would find amid the oppressions that were to purify them, and tied closely enough to the earlier vision to count as its further unfolding. Clarke agrees that this and the two chapters after it form one last vision, and notices that the divine person who appears here is not unlike the one seen by the apostle in Patmos. The date divides them. Gill reckons the third year not of Persia only but of the whole Medo-Persian empire, and not from the taking of Babylon but from the death of the uncle with whom Cyrus had jointly reigned. Clarke says flatly that it answers to the first year of Darius the Mede; Henry counts from the conquest of Babylon.

Henry takes the thing was true as a solemn attestation on the prophet's own word, and reads the length of the appointed time as duration — as far as the end of the reign of Antiochus, three hundred years. Clarke and Ellicott render the word differently: the appointed time is a warfare, and Clarke expects many contentions and wars before these things are accomplished, while Ellicott, noting that the same word is elsewhere translated warfare, makes the subject of the revelation truth and long tribulation, and extends that warfare beyond Israel to all God's people before the Messiah comes in his kingdom. They divide too over how much the prophet grasped. Henry says it was made as plain as history rather than prophecy, and worked upon his understanding rather than his fancy; Ellicott replies that a later chapter shows the whole was not understood, the duration of the tribulation in particular never being clearly revealed.

Why he mourned three weeks is answered variously. Calvin gives the sharpest account: the rebuilding had just been stopped, Cyrus being away in Asia Minor at war with the Scythians while his son, corrupted by his courtiers, forbade the Jews to go on with city and temple; and since the prophets had promised a return with standards unfurled and a glory for the second house, the people might well conclude they had been deluded and their expectations turned into a laughing-stock. Gill offers instead the seventy weeks lately revealed, or the many who stayed in Babylon when free to leave. Wesley makes it the calamities foreseen as coming on the nation for its sins. Ellicott thinks it needless to trace the fast to breaches of the passover ritual, and points to the factious opposition offered to the returned colonists. Henry has him mourning for his own sins as well as his people's.

Of the abstinence itself Gill says the bread of desires means the finest of the wheat, such as was eaten in the courts of princes where he lived, and that he took coarse black grain instead. Clarke calls it a general abstinence rather than a fast: unsavoury food, nothing but water, no bath, and most probably haircloth next the skin throughout. Ellicott adds the oil, taking the refusal of delicate food and of anointing together as the outward signs of grief. Calvin marks the weeks, thinking the word days inserted on purpose to keep the reader from confusing three weeks of days with the seventy weeks of years just expounded. He also weighs the double name, rejecting both the guess that Belteshazzar records an honour and the guess that it commends his abilities: the prophet meant to make the prophecy known throughout the regions where he went by that name, and to testify that a foreign name had not cut him off from the Church.
4:
Calvin reads the completed fast as preparation for prayer rather than an act of obedience in itself: the abstinence testified grief and roused him to pray. Gill counts the days and draws a consequence — the fast ran from the third of the month to the twenty-fourth, so the passover fell inside it and appears not to have been kept, perhaps because Jews in a foreign land did not then observe it. On the river the voices agree and then part. Wesley identifies the month as Nisan and the Hiddekel as the Tigris; Clarke does the same; Calvin notes that the Hebrew word for hand is used metaphorically for the bank. Ellicott objects that the epithet great river usually belongs to the Euphrates, gives Hiddekel as the Accadian name, and insists the prophet was there in the body and not merely in the spirit as at the earlier vision, where Calvin leaves it uncertain whether he was in that region at all.

Who the man clothed in linen is divides them sharply. Ellicott presses the identification hardest: the dress recalls the clothing of the high priest, the figure is carefully distinguished from Michael and, by the prophet's silence, from Gabriel too, and he is the same one seen in the earlier vision, to be regarded as the Angel of God, or God's Presence, or God's Name, in fact the One who was the Logos. Wesley says very probably Christ, appearing in royal and priestly robes and in great brightness and majesty. Clarke notes only that the description is very like that of our Lord in the apocalyptic vision, and Gill reads the sky colour of the stone as signifying that he was the Lord from heaven. Calvin will not go there. He calls the figure an angel, and explains that angels are called men metaphorically whenever God clothes them in that outward form; he judges it a gross error to suppose that angels become men whenever they are corporeally visible.

The stone breeds its own dispute. Keil and Delitzsch identify it with the chrysolite of the older nomenclature and the topaz of the newer, and Ellicott likewise makes it a variety of the topaz. Calvin reports the chrysolite opinion, and beside it the view that the word denotes the colour of the sea, and the further suggestion that it means sky-coloured. Gill lays out three readings and their reasons: the beryl, said to be azure and sky-coloured, though by its name it ought rather to be sea-green; the sardonyx, preferred by one interpreter as a flesh colour fitter to express the comeliness of a human body, the beryl being too different a colour for that; and the chrysolite, urged by another on the ground that the girdle blazed so that the body about it looked as if it were all of gold.

On the gold of Uphaz, Clarke says simply that it is the same as Ophir. Ellicott answers that Uphaz is named only here and in one prophet and that its locality is unknown. Calvin argues the question out: he rejects the derivation that would make the word an epithet meaning pure, and holds on the strength of that prophet's usage that it is the proper name of a region, noting that some have accordingly rendered it Ophir. Keil and Delitzsch supply the rest of the figure without dispute — the countenance like lightning, the eyes as lamps of fire, the arms and the place of the feet like burnished brass, and they take that last phrase strictly, since it names the part of the frame where the feet are and so implies that the lower body and not the feet alone shone; the sound of his speaking they compare with the voice of a multitude heard by an earlier prophet.
7:
All five treat the solitude of the seeing as deliberate. Gill says he was not alone but saw alone, the eyes of his body and mind being quicker because the Lord strengthened and enlightened both, a peculiar and distinguishing favour; and he reads the panic of his companions as wisely ordered, so that once they were gone he might have the secrets of the Lord revealed to him. Keil and Delitzsch put it that the form was visible to him only, while the others were so alarmed by the invisible nearness of the heavenly being that they fled and hid. Calvin sets the whole narrative in its purpose: the prophet seems prolix but writes so by design, because a prophecy of this weight required every kind of sanction to command unhesitating confidence, not from that generation only but from all posterity. Four of them reach for the same parallel, the men who travelled with the apostle to Damascus, Ellicott citing Jerome for the comparison.

What the companions perceived divides them four ways. Ellicott says they heard the voice but saw nothing, and observes that the words spoken are nowhere recorded. Calvin holds that they caught only a confused sound and did not understand the language, adding that the prophet's hearing was no better than theirs but that God meant to address him alone, so that a voice like the noise of a multitude did not penetrate their ears. Clarke has them all feeling a divine influence while only one saw the corporeal appearance. Keil and Delitzsch reject the whole class of such readings: the opinion that the men did not see the angel but heard his voice is simply incorrect, since the voice was not heard until after they had fled. They add that no thunder and lightning need be supposed to account for the flight, the text mentioning none.

On the collapse that followed, Keil and Delitzsch note that he calls this appearance great with reference to a majesty never known to him before, so that its effect on him exceeds that of the angel who had come to him earlier, and the expression used here for his stupor is stronger than the one used then. The splendour that failed, they explain, is the fresh colour of life in his countenance, changed properly to destruction, to entire disfigurement. Ellicott says plainly that he grew pale with terror and fainted, and marks again that the prophet is distinguishing this from former visions because the glory of the man was far beyond anything he had witnessed. Gill calls the vision great in both respects, for the person seen and for the matter afterwards revealed; and he insists that even in that low condition the prophet could still attend to the voice, hear the sounds articulately, and understand what was said.

Calvin asks what the prostration was for. The outward signs, he answers, do more than exhibit God speaking by the mouth of his angel: they prepared the prophet himself and trained him to reverence. God does not terrify his children because our disquiet is any delight to him, but only because it profits us, since we are never fit to receive improvement until our carnal feelings are subdued, and inborn perverseness makes that a violent business. Hence a man reduced to lifelessness, his beauty turned to a deformity like that which death induces, with scarcely enough vitality left to keep him from actually dying. Of the recovery Calvin is equally exact: the touch set him on his knees with his hands still on the ground, a posture that is itself a sign of dejection and not yet standing or sitting; and the lesson is that when the voice of God has prostrated us we cannot be raised except by his strength, the hand being the symbol of it.
10:
Whose hand it was that touched him is disputed three ways. Gill denies it can be the hand of the man clothed in linen, whose hand was like polished brass, and makes it the hand of one of his attendants, distinct from him, having the similitude of the sons of men and a hand softer and nearer a human one — very probably Gabriel, who had touched him before. Ellicott says the opposite in a line: this hand was that of the person who appeared, though it is spoken of as felt and not as seen. Clarke takes a third course. Nothing was apparent or palpable but a hand; a hand had written Belshazzar's fate on the wall, and the hand is frequently named where the power or majesty of God is meant, so that perhaps by the hand God himself is intended — and he notes an ancient copy of the Septuagint in Vienna whose paintings represent every appearance of God by a hand in the clouds.

The recovery came by stages, and all four who describe it insist on the stages. Keil and Delitzsch say the touch raised him and made him reel on his knees and hands but did not enable him to stand erect, which he could do only after hearing the comfortable words. Calvin puts the same thing as a series of steps: the prophet was not quite prostrate, his face toward the earth while his hands and knees bore him, and here we see him raised another step. Henry draws the lesson out. Strength and comfort commonly come by degrees to those long cast down; they are first helped up a little and then more, and we must not despise the day of small things but be thankful for the beginnings of mercy. Afterwards he is helped to his feet, but stands trembling for fear he should fall again, since before God gives strength he makes his people sensible of their own weakness.

On the title given him the voices differ over its direction. Gill renders it a man of desires, lovely to God and men, and takes it as evidence for his identification of the speaker, since it is the epithet Gabriel had used before. Calvin reports a reading that takes the word passively of the prophet's own zeal, as though he were named for the invincible ardour with which anxiety for the common welfare of the Church had filled him, and inclines instead to the opposite: he was so called because he was dear and precious to God, and the angel used the epithet to animate him and quiet his mind for what he was waiting to hear. Ellicott observes only that the assuring words enabled him to stand upright while his alarm had not yet subsided.

Calvin makes the command not to fear a measured thing rather than an abolition of fear. The angel did not wish to remove all dread but to calm it, lest trembling should keep the prophet from attending; for God knows fear to be useful and does not want us wholly free of it, since too great self-confidence breeds slothfulness and pride, and he means our fears to restrain us like a bridle while he moderates them so that our minds are not so stricken that we cannot approach him calmly. Gill reads the same words as spoken on sight of the trembling, to make him more capable of attending. Clarke and Ellicott turn to the reason offered with them: the messenger came on account of the prayers, and the answer was granted from the first day the request to understand what should befall his people was made, though it had been impossible to realise that answer until now, for a reason the next verse supplies.
13:
The prince of the kingdom of Persia is the great crux, and the voices take four positions. Gill argues by elimination: not the reigning king, since Cyrus or his son would be styled king rather than prince and neither could withstand an angel; not the good tutelary spirit of the realm, since it is unreasonable that good angels should militate against one another; therefore an evil angel, Satan himself or one of his chief officers set to do what mischief he could in the Persian court against the Jews,. Ellicott stands on the same ground but builds it into doctrine, calling this perhaps the clearest verse in Scripture on the invisible powers that rule and influence nations: as spiritual beings execute God's purpose in the natural and moral worlds, so also in the political, and the princes of the heathen powers are devils. Clarke refuses both. To make it either a good or an evil angel, he says, would turn an important place into a legend.

Clarke's own reading is that Cyrus alone was the prince of Persia, destined by God to deliver the people, who for reasons not disclosed hesitated — probably fearing the greatness of the work and doubting his own sufficiency for it — and so for a time resisted the secret inspirations sent him, the opposition perhaps concerning the rebuilding of the temple. Wesley keeps the human reading but changes the man: God suffered the wicked counsels of Cambyses to prevail for a while, until prayer on the one side and angelic power on the other overcame him, and Wesley makes that very defeat the foundation of the later ruin of the Persian monarchy. On Michael they divide again. Keil and Delitzsch leave him as one of the chief princes. Clarke notes that the name means one who is like God, that it sometimes signifies the Messiah and sometimes the highest archangel, and that no other archangel is named anywhere in Scripture; Wesley reports simply that Michael here is commonly supposed to mean Christ.

Calvin takes the verse as an answer to a complaint the prophet might have made — what treatment is this, to let me waste away in grief three weeks together, when God heard me from the first day? The angel meets it by showing he had been otherwise occupied in promoting the man's welfare, and Calvin presses the practical use hard. Delay disturbs us when help is not immediate and the fruit of our prayers is long hidden; against that impatience we should set this sentence, for prayers may already be heard while the favour that answers them is concealed. He notes as well the condescension of it, that God should deign to excuse the delay to his own servant, and draws the inference that God does not cease to regard us while he declines to make us conscious of it, providing for our safety in ways that surpass our comprehension.

What the coming revelation covers is the last question. Keil and Delitzsch identify the latter days with the Messianic world-time, elsewhere called the time of the end, and say the vision stretches out to those days; they correct one interpreter who supposed the angel meant the revelations already given. Ellicott agrees that the phrase means the period when the following vision receives its complete fulfilment, and insists there is no reference to preceding visions except so far as what follows develops details of them. Gill reads it more concretely as the succeeding monarchies, especially the times of Antiochus, and indeed all that should befall the nation until the Messiah came, the last days generally designing his days. Clarke says only that much remains to be revealed and the time of its accomplishment is very distant.
15:
Keil and Delitzsch read these verses as the record of a man being raised by degrees and made capable of receiving the revelation, the angel's words having not yet fully done it: he stood trembling, his face bent toward the earth, and he was still speechless. Clarke notes the change of posture precisely — he had been standing upright, and now bends his body in reverence and looks down — and adds that he simply found himself unable to speak. Wesley reads a full prostration and puts the dumbness down to astonishment. Ellicott refuses to call any of it fear, since fear had already been driven away, and ascribes the posture instead to reverence for the majestic person before him and to gratitude for the answer given to his prayer. Calvin agrees that reverence for the angel made him unable to stand, and dismisses as much too forced the expositors who take the phrase for a repenting of his prophetic office on the supposition that his prayers had been disregarded.

Who touched his lips is disputed. Gill denies it was the man clothed in linen and makes it either Gabriel appearing more manifestly in human form or another of the attendants having the similitude of a man; Clarke and Wesley both name Gabriel outright. Ellicott sees no reason to suppose this person different from the one who had touched him before. Calvin concedes that the words seem to introduce another angel, but holds that as the chapter proceeds it will appear to be the same one throughout, and he explains the odd phrasing: the messenger had earlier been called simply a man, and is now said to bear the similitude of the sons of man in order to mark him as human in form and not in nature. He adds that some restrict the figure to Christ, and fears that reading too forced.

The complaint that follows turns on how many superiors are in view. Gill takes the doubled address to point past the speaker: the prophet gestures at the glorious one whom he knew to be more than a man, while reckoning himself the servant of the angel who had touched him and was conversing with him, and asks what a creature of dust and ashes has to do with such a one. Ellicott, holding the persons to be one, regards the whole verse as addressed to the angel, and compares the fear that seized Isaiah at his own vision. Keil and Delitzsch let the difficulty stand in its own terms: he may not talk with the one who had appeared in such dread majesty, and is in such a case, all strength gone and his breath departed, that he fears he must die. Clarke has him almost suffocated with sorrow, and takes the vision that afflicts him to be the one already given, whose meaning he does not yet possess but whose calamities for his people he can see.

On the second touch and the strengthening the accounts converge. Calvin makes the point that the angel who inflicted the wound brought the remedy, and denies any virtue in the touch itself, God having always encouraged the use of symbols; the whole apparatus, he says, exists to stamp the prophecy with authority, and is needed because Satan transforms himself into an angel of light, so that God marks this prediction off from his fallacies by fixed credentials. Clarke renders the title man of delights, and paraphrases the answer as a declaration that he is now strengthened enough to bear any revelation. Calvin glosses the greeting as the customary Hebrew salutation, meaning prosperity and quiet, and takes it as the angel's testimony that he came in the prophet's favour, bearing witness to God's merciful disposition toward the people and to the reception of the prayers.
20:
Why the messenger asks a question whose answer he has already given is variously explained. Gill supposes the prophet, in the hurry of his spirits, may not have taken it in or may have forgotten it, so that the question stirs up his desire for the particulars. Calvin thinks the disturbance of feeling had temporarily disarranged the calmness of his thoughts, and that the preface gathers together senses that had been wandering and dispersed. Ellicott finds the verse obscure but infers from the form of the question that the prophet was perfectly aware of the reason, and reads what follows as a preparation of his mind, by naming the spiritual powers set over Greece, for the troublous times of the Macedonian supremacy. Clarke turns it into a compliment and an apology at once: so high is this man in God's favour that the messenger was sent to satisfy him even while employed on a most important mission elsewhere.

What that returning fight is remains the old division. Gill keeps the evil spirit of the Persian court, and traces its work in the interval — the king and his counsellors made careless of the Jews' affairs, so that the building of city and temple went on slowly. Clarke keeps Cyrus, and argues the point from the improbability of his decree: he had no natural or political inclination to favour the Jews, so nothing less than a supernatural agency on his mind will account for it, and his reluctance to obey the heavenly motions is what is here pictured as a fight. Wesley says only that it was to oppose mischievous designs. Ellicott generalises it into the providence that watched over Israel throughout the Persian sovereignty. On the prince of Grecia, Clarke names Alexander, who was to destroy the Persian empire; Calvin rejects outright the interpretation that makes the Greek come forward because God ceased after the angel's departure to assist the Persian kingdom.

The scripture of truth splits them cleanly. Gill denies it means the written word: these are the decrees and purposes of God, signified by a book because they are so particular and so certain, noted and engraven in the eternal mind, and they are among the deep things which angels themselves do not know until they are revealed. Keil and Delitzsch describe it as the book in which God has designated beforehand, according to truth, the history of the world as it shall certainly be unfolded. Calvin presses the same reading to its ground: the phrase means the eternal and inviolable decree, and the figure is drawn from human custom, since paper and books are helps to a memory that lets things slip, whereas God never suffers from forgetfulness and therefore needs no books. Clarke and Ellicott take the other road, referring it to revelations already made or shortly to be made, Clarke thinking of the earlier visions this prophet had written down and did not fully understand.

Michael divides them once more. Wesley makes him Christ, the sole protector of the church when all the princes of the earth desert or oppose it. Clarke keeps him an archangel, always supposed to be appointed guardian of the Jewish nation, and reasons that since angels can be in only one place at a time, one or another had to be present with the Persian king by turns — then checks himself, since we know so little of the invisible world that nothing can safely be affirmed. Ellicott reads the clause as a further ground of encouragement, the champion who stood up for Israel under the Persian troubles proving strong against the powers that lead Greece. Keil and Delitzsch, weighing the adversative that opens the verse, reject the view that the prophecy can now contain only calamity, since it contains war and victory too.
